examples.question_text:
Two circular objects were measured.
a) The first has circumference $53.3$ cm and diameter $17$ cm.
b) The second has circumference $56.5$ cm and radius $9$ cm.
Calculate $C \div d$ for each, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
a)
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{C}{d}\\&=\frac{53.3}{17}\\&=3.135294\ldots\\&\approx3.14\end{aligned}$
b) $d = 2 \times 9 = 18$ cm.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{C}{d}\\&=\frac{56.5}{18}\\&=3.138888\ldots\\&\approx3.14\end{aligned}$
Both measurements give an estimate close to $\pi$.

examples.question_text:
Three circular objects were measured.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object} & C\text{ (cm)} & d\text{ (cm)} \\ \hline A & 22.0 & 7 \\ B & 59.7 & 19 \\ C & 46.8 & 13 \end{array}$
a) Calculate $C \div d$ for each, correct to $2$ decimal places.
b) Explain why the different sizes of A and B do not give different values of $\pi$.
c) Which object has a measurement far from its correct value?
examples.solution_text:
a) A: $\frac{22.0}{7} = 3.142857\ldots \approx 3.14$
B: $\frac{59.7}{19} = 3.142105\ldots \approx 3.14$
C: $\frac{46.8}{13} = 3.6 = 3.60$
b) For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is the same number, $\pi$.
Both A and B give measured ratios close to $\pi$.
c) Object C gives $3.60$, far from $3.14$, so one of its measurements is inaccurate.

a) $\pi = \frac{C}{d}$.
b) Since $\pi = 3.14159\ldots$, just over $3$ diameter lengths fit around the circumference.
The radius is half the diameter, so dividing by the radius doubles the answer: $\frac{C}{r} = 2\pi$.
c) $\pi = 3.14159\ldots$
To $3$ decimal places, $\pi \approx 3.142$.
To $4$ decimal places, $\pi \approx 3.1416$.
